title: Nobody Has Ever Named the Boy in This Painting
standfirst: Tate's own catalogue entry runs to a single line, and it doesn't say which of Queen Victoria's eighty-seven great-grandchildren is sitting beside her. Nothing else written about the picture does either — and the gaps turn out to be the most honest way into it.

sections.heading: Nobody Has Ever Named the Boy in This Painting
sections.body:
Tate's own entry for this picture runs to a title, an artist and a circa date. Art UK, which tags its collection down to individual sitters wherever it can, marks this one only "People: Victoria, Queen" — there is no comparable tag for the child beside her. [Wikidata's structured record](https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Q119247992) of the work carries a Tate accession number and a lending date and nothing that answers the question the title itself raises: which great-grandson? [Tate](https://www.tate.org.uk/art/artworks/sickert-queen-victoria-and-her-great-grandson-l02670) doesn't say. [Art UK](https://artuk.org/discover/artworks/queen-victoria-and-her-great-grandson-201828) doesn't say.

It isn't a small field to choose from. By the time Victoria died in January 1901 she had [eighty-seven great-grandchildren, eighty-four of whom survived birth](https://www.unofficialroyalty.com/queen-victorias-great-grandchildren/). One of them left an unusually clear paper trail with her: Prince Edward of York, later Edward VIII, later the Duke of Windsor, photographed in his great-grandmother's arms at his christening at White Lodge in 1894, in an image later described as catching [three generations of direct successors alive at once](https://royalcentral.co.uk/features/royal-pictures-from-history-queen-victoria-and-three-generations-of-kings-118391/) — Victoria, his grandfather the future Edward VII, his father the future George V, and the baby who would grow up to complete that line of four monarchs, briefly, before abdicating within the year. That makes him the best-documented candidate. It does not make him the boy in this painting. No institution that has catalogued the work has put a name to the child, and this feature isn't going to invent one either.

sections.heading: By 1936, Sickert Had Stopped Drawing From Life Entirely
sections.body:
In the mid-1920s Sickert gave up working from a live sitter. Around the same time — 1927 — he decided he'd had enough of being called Walter, and began signing his work and asking to be known as Richard Sickert instead. From then on, a painting started life as a photograph: a snapshot taken by his third wife, Thérèse Lessore, or a picture cut from a newspaper, squared into a grid and copied up onto canvas, the pencil lines sometimes left visible in the finished work. The subjects ranged from Victorian magazine illustrations he called his "English Echoes" to genuinely current events — [he worked from a press photograph of Amelia Earhart's solo Atlantic crossing in May 1932](https://www.tate.org.uk/whats-on/tate-britain/walter-sickert/exhibition-guide), an ocean and a news cycle away from anything he'd witnessed himself.

A queen who had been dead for thirty-five years fits that method exactly. Nobody sat for this. Somebody handed Sickert an old photograph, and he copied it, the same way he was copying wire pictures of aviators and stills of actresses he'd never met.

sections.heading: The Corpus Calls This Impressionism. It Fits Nine of His Ten Paintings Here.
sections.body:
This site's own catalogue tags the picture Impressionism — the same label it gives the other nine Sickert works it holds, all of them from 1891 to 1914, the decades when Sickert really was working in Whistler and Degas's shadow: fast, informal, built from direct observation in broken colour. None of that describes how "Queen Victoria and her great-grandson" was made twenty-plus years later. [Wikipedia's account of this period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Sickert) doesn't reach for Impressionism at all — it describes a method, photograph to grid to studio copy, that is now treated as a forerunner of what Chuck Close and Gerhard Richter would do with paint and photography three and four decades further on.

The label fits nine-tenths of this catalogue's Sickert entries. It landed on the tenth by the same automatic rule that put it on the other nine, not because anyone checked whether a man who had stopped drawing from life was still, technically, an Impressionist.

sections.heading: His Wife Took the Photographs, Squared Them Up, and Sometimes Finished the Painting
sections.body:
Thérèse Lessore trained at the Slade, won its Melville Nettleship Prize for figure composition, and painted the same kind of urban, domestic scenes as the Camden Town Group — the circle Sickert had helped found. She was refused membership anyway; the group did not admit women. [She helped found the London Group instead, in 1913](https://www.liverpoolmuseums.org.uk/stories/10-things-you-should-know-about-therese-lessore), so painters shut out of the old channels would have one of their own.

She married Sickert in 1926, when his health was already failing; a friend of the couple later suggested the marriage was as much about entitling her to a Royal Academy widow's pension as anything else. What followed was less assistant-to-master than a slow transfer of labour. Lessore took the photographs Sickert worked from, squared them up for transfer to canvas, and, as his health worsened further, finished paintings he could not complete himself — their late styles converged so closely that some of her own paintings have since been mistaken for his. None of that is disclosed anywhere in this picture's own catalogue entry. There is no record of whether a second hand touched "Queen Victoria and her great-grandson"; there is only the general rule that, by the mid-1930s, whatever left Sickert's studio was rarely his alone.

sections.heading: He Resigned From the Academy in Protest Not Long Before He Painted This
sections.body:
Sickert was elected a full Royal Academician in March 1934 — a late, formal embrace from an institution he'd spent much of his career agitating against. He lasted just over a year. On 9 May 1935 he resigned, protesting the Academy president's refusal to back the preservation of Jacob Epstein's eighteen nude reliefs on the former British Medical Association building on the Strand.

Epstein had carved the figures in 1907–08 for the architect Charles Holden, who wanted "noble and heroic forms to express... the great primal facts of man and woman." Their [1908 unveiling provoked an enormous public furore](https://artuk.org/discover/stories/how-jacob-epsteins-early-works-revolutionised-british-sculpture), most of it aimed at the exposed breast of a figure called Maternity. By the 1930s the argument had shifted from morality to safety: thirty years of London smog had weakened the stone, and after part of one figure fell into the street in 1937, the [building's new owners had every projecting face, arm and foot chiselled flat](https://www.tate.org.uk/art/artists/sir-jacob-epstein-1061/lost-art-jacob-epstein). Epstein called it "blatant vandalism." Sickert, who by then had stopped drawing from life and was working up a nostalgic little portrait of a dead queen from an old photograph, still had enough fight in him to walk out of the Academy over someone else's stonework.

sections.heading: This Painting Has Almost No Recorded Public Life
sections.body:
Tate does not own this picture. Its accession number carries the prefix Tate reserves for works it holds only on loan, and the record states plainly that it has been [lent from a private collection since 2006](https://artuk.org/discover/artworks/queen-victoria-and-her-great-grandson-201828) — roughly seventy years after Sickert painted it, spent somewhere off the public record entirely, its owner unnamed. Search for the picture under its own title and nothing else surfaces: no review, no auction result, no exhibition essay built around it. What exists is two short institutional entries and a Wikidata stub.

That is a thin record for a painting of the most photographed monarch of the nineteenth century, made by an artist whose late, photograph-based method is now taken seriously as a forerunner of how painting would later use photography. The gaps here aren't incidental to the story — the unnamed boy, the uncredited second hand that may have touched the canvas, the picture's near-total absence from print — they are what is actually verifiable about it. Where a record runs this thin, saying so plainly beats filling the silence with something that merely sounds right.
